column9: Sotah 14a: ‘Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, says: Even Moses our teacher himself does not know where he is buried. column13: “These are the generations of Noah, etc.” It is written (Job 26:11): “The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at His rebuke.” This verse refers to the devastation of the Flood, for through the rebuke Hashem struck against the Generation of the Flood, creation was fortified. For rebuke is one of the ten instruments through which the Holy One created the world (Chagigah 12a); and this cosmic rebuke occurred during the Flood, after which the foundations of creation were strengthened, having previously been fragile and unsteady.

column9: Berakhot 54a: ‘The mishna articulates a general principle: One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him, as it is stated: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). The mishna explains this verse as follows: “With all your heart” means with your two inclinations, with your good inclination and your evil inclination, both of which must be subjugated to the love of God. “With all your soul” means even if God takes your soul. “And with all your might” means with all your money, as money is referred to in the Bible as might. Alternatively, it may…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 4 — Noach, Adam, and Three Mitzvot of Repair, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 54a) to illuminate his statement here (“as stated at the start of chapter HaRoeh (Berakhot 54a); and the conduct of the good inclination. And he enumerated them in the order of development: for the neshamah is placed in man from the moment of conception,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

column13: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the likeness of God made He him, etc. The mystical secret of this concept is 'image' (tzelem) and 'likeness' (demut): image signifies the bare essence of life without any outward expansion, just as an infant, immediately when born at the first moment, is termed 'image'; and afterward, when he begins to expand in his desires, such as the longing for nourishment, and through that craving he eats, and life expands within him each time more and more until he grows large in breadth and stature, this expansion is termed 'likeness'.

column9: Berakhot 10b: ‘Abaye, and some say Rabbi Yitzḥak, said: A great man who seeks to enjoy the contributions of those who seek to honor him may enjoy those gifts, as Elisha enjoyed gifts given him by the woman from Shunem, among others. And one who does not seek to enjoy these gifts should not enjoy them, as was the practice of the prophet Samuel from Rama, who would not accept gifts from anyone at all. From where do we know that this was Samuel’s custom? As it is stated: “And he returned to Rama, for there was his house, and there he judged Israel, and he built an altar to the Lord” (I Samuel 7:17). And similarly, Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Every place where Samuel went, his house was with him, so he would have…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 4 — Noach, Adam, and Three Mitzvot of Repair, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 10b) to illuminate his statement here (“and likewise (there, 10b): " ‘Let one not withhold himself from mercy, etc., for he fears God’, the terminology of fear is expounded regarding prayer and mercy; and so too it was expounded (there, 6b): "' – ‘"Who...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

And regarding Isaac, the term sichah (conversation) is employed for the first time, for he was the first to merit that all his casual speech became Torah, mirroring the trait of the scholar, which transpired upon Rebecca's arrival, at which point he attained the completeness of a fully realized person.

column9: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 1. English translation of source: “‘Our teachers taught: For three transgressions women die at the time of childbirth. All three have their basis in the Torah: niddah, as it is written, ‘If a woman has a flow [of blood]’; challah, ‘The first of your dough’; and the lighting of a lamp, as it is written, ‘You shall call Shabbos a delight’—this refers to kindling the Shabbos lamp. If you should say that one might sit in darkness, that is not delight, for those who descend to Gehinnom are judged in darkness, as it says, ‘A land of deepest gloom, like darkness.’’ The Midrash continues: ‘Why were women commanded concerning these three mitzvos? ... She caused [Adam] to die and shed his blood ... She defiled the challah of the world ... She extinguished Adam’s lamp, as it is written, ‘The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord’; therefore she must attend to kindling the lamp.’” Context and connection: The source develops both sides of Rav Tzadok’s argument: the three practices address the loss introduced by the first sin, while light is the positive image of Shabbos restoration. The relevant lamp passage occurs in Noach 1 in the commonly indexed Sefaria edition; Rav Tzadok's printed numbering differs.
column11: Connection to this footnote: This text cites the same Tanchuma passage and makes its application to Shabbos candle-lighting explicit.

column9: Job 10:21–22. English translation of source: “‘Before I depart—and do not return—to the land of darkness and the shadow of death: a land of thick gloom, like utter darkness; of deathly shadow and disorder, where even its radiance is like darkness.’” Context and connection: The surrounding verse describes the realm of death, not the laws of Shabbos. Tanchuma borrows this vivid image for Gehinnom. Rav Tzadok then treats the light of a Shabbos lamp as more than physical convenience: it represents an opposite spiritual condition, one of order, comfort and revealed divine presence.
column11: Connection to this footnote: Darkness becomes the starting point of spiritual illumination, rather than merely an image of punishment.

column13: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 1:3–4: “And in truth, the essential seeking of man is that which he inquires and strives to establish holiness upon the physical body as well, and this is termed “the renewal of the moon” [the moon representing the receptive vessel and physical existence]. However, this is the reason the Torah opened with “Bereishit” (Creation); for in truth it is written: “And darkness was upon the face of the deep,” and my revered grandfather, my master and teacher, of blessed memory, raised a difficulty: For whom was there darkness at that time? Is it not written concerning Hashem (Psalms 139:12): “Even darkness obscures not from You, and the night shines like the day; darkness is as light”!” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 1:3–4 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 5 — Shabbat Lights and the Restoration of the Soul.

column9: Genesis 1:2; Midrash Tanchuma, Bo 2. English translation of source: “Genesis 1:2: ‘The earth was unformed and empty, darkness was over the face of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.’ Midrash Tanchuma, Bo 2: ‘Rabbi Nechemiah said: [The darkness of Egypt came] from the darkness of Gehinnom, for it is said, ‘A land of thick gloom, like darkness, of deathly shadow and no order.’ ... With what are the wicked covered in Gehinnom? With darkness. Just as an earthenware jar is covered with an earthenware lid, so these wicked ones, whose deeds are in the dark, are covered by the Holy One, blessed be He, with the deep, which is darkness, as it says: ‘And darkness was upon the face of the deep.’ This is Gehinnom.’” Context and connection: In the verse, darkness precedes creation’s illumination. In the Midrash it becomes a moral image: a person concealed in wrongdoing encounters concealment. Rav Tzadok juxtaposes this with the contrary possibility that divine judgment may awaken recognition and thereby itself be experienced as light.
column11: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Likkutei Maamarim 1-16:38 (§7): “Through its union with the soul, whose primary core is the faculty of Chokhmah, as is known that the souls of Israel derive from the letters of the Torah. And they were the sixty myriad souls of the Generation of the Wilderness, and the souls of subsequent generations derive from the renewal of the Oral Torah in that generation; and therefore the primary reception of true conception from the perspective of the living soul is through the letter Hei of Nisan; whereas the letter Kuf, which alludes to bodily conception.” Connection to this note: In Likkutei Maamarim 1-16:38 (§7), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 5 — Shabbat Lights and the Restoration of the Soul.

column9: Pesachim 54a. English translation of source: “‘This is no difficulty: one statement concerns our fire and one concerns the fire of Gehinnom. Our fire [was created] at the close of Shabbos; the fire of Gehinnom, on the eve of Shabbos. But was the fire of Gehinnom created on the eve of Shabbos? Was it not taught that seven things were created before the world: the Torah, repentance, the Garden of Eden, Gehinnom, the Throne of Glory, the Sanctuary, and the name of the Messiah? ... Rabbi Yose says: The fire created by the Holy One, blessed be He, on the second day never goes out, as it says, ‘Their fire shall not be quenched.’ ... Why was ‘for it was good’ not said on the second day? Because the fire of Gehinnom was created then.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok deliberately focuses on the expression ‘the light of Gehinnom.’ He is not denying its punitive aspect. He argues that for one who accepts the truth of the judgment, the confrontation can illuminate what was previously hidden. The paradox depends on distinguishing revelatory light from the comfort of an ordinary flame.
column11: Connection to this footnote: This parallels Rav Tzadok’s reversal of Gehinnom imagery: a destructive fire can be countered by the inner fire of avodas Hashem.

column9: Eruvin 19a; Isaiah 66:24. English translation of source: “‘But did Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish not say: The wicked do not return in repentance even at the entrance to Gehinnom, as it is said, ‘They shall go out and look upon the corpses of the men who rebel against Me’ [Isaiah 66:24]? There is no difficulty: this statement concerns the sinners of Israel, and that statement the sinners of the nations of the world.’” Context and connection: The distinction concerns how suffering is received, not merely whether punishment is severe. Rav Tzadok uses the sugya to explain that for a person who refuses teshuvah, judgment remains darkness because it produces no renewed recognition of Hashem.
column11: Connection to this footnote: This explains how the inner response of teshuvah, rather than continued defiance, changes the spiritual meaning of sin. The opening bracket supplies only the antecedent of the excerpt.

column9: Eruvin 19a; Psalms 84:7. English translation of source: “‘What, then, of the verse, ‘Those who pass through the valley of weeping make it a spring’ [Psalm 84:7]? That refers to those who are then liable to punishment in Gehinnom; but our father Avraham comes, raises them up, and receives them. He does not leave the circumcised among Israel [there], except for one who entered a forbidden union with a gentile woman; his foreskin is drawn over, and Avraham does not recognize him.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok draws attention to the limited character of punishment in this account, contrasting it with perpetual obstinacy. The sugya provides the language of Avraham’s rescue; the further interpretation that acknowledgment of judgment itself becomes light is Rav Tzadok’s explanation.
column11: Connection to this footnote: Shabbos becomes an occasion for return and inward liberation, complementing the Gemara’s image of rescue.

column9: Shabbat 32a; Proverbs 20:27. English translation of source: “‘I called you ‘first,’ and I warned you concerning the first [of your dough]. The soul I placed within you is called a ‘lamp,’ and I warned you concerning the lamp. If you observe these commandments, well and good; but if not, I shall take your soul.’ The verse cited for the image is Proverbs 20:27: ‘The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the chambers of the belly.’” Context and connection: The Gemara’s immediate discussion concerns care in three mitzvos and the gravity of neglect. Rav Tzadok reads their deeper structure: niddah repairs ruach and blood, challah relates to the earthly nefesh, and Shabbos light addresses the neshamah. This threefold correspondence is his interpretation, not the Gemara’s explicit enumeration of soul-levels.

And as it is written (Genesis 2:6): “And a mist went up from the earth”—referring to the yearning cry rising from the shattered worlds, as taught in Tikkunei HaZohar (Tikkun 52, 87a): “Ed” represents the letters Aleph-Dalet of the Name Adonai; come and see: an arousal from below to above is required first, and only afterward “and watered the whole face of the ground.”” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 15:7–9 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 5 — Shabbat Lights and the Restoration of the Soul.

column9: Genesis 2:6–7; 1:24. English translation of source: “Genesis 2:6–7: ‘A mist rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground. Then the Lord God formed the human being from dust of the ground, breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human became a living soul.’ Genesis 1:24: ‘God said: Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds; and it was so.’” Context and connection: The Midrash likens the first human’s formation to the making of dough. Rav Tzadok therefore associates challah—separating sanctity from flour and water—with the repair of nefesh, the vital force within embodied life. The analogy goes beyond the literal wording of Bereishis.
column11: Connection to this footnote: Challah is explained not only as Adam’s original dough but also as repairing separation by sanctifying a unified whole.

column9: Zohar, Shemot 18:192-20:202: ‘From which it is evident that all the righteous are known by all in those higher regions before their souls descend into this world; how much more, then, Moses. The foreskin (orlah) represents the manifest root of evil created in the cosmos as an encompassing garment. God made man upright (Koheles 7:29) and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life (Bereishis 2:7), and "he who breathes forth, breathes from within his innermost essence".

column11: Even in their sleep the flea did not bite them, meaning there was nothing painful to disrupt their cleaving; which derived from the holy impression (reshimu) enduring from the counting of the 49 preceding days manifest even during sleep; and this holy impression is the application of the Counting upon the fiftieth day in potentiality, even though not in verbal deed; for within it is revealed through this enduring impression the full potency of all preceding days of counting; and through this is constructed within his heart the root human awakening for receiving the Torah.

Once Adam sinned, the Holy One, Blessed be He, placed His hand on him and diminished him, as it is stated: “Behind and before You have created me and laid Your hand upon me” (Psalms 139:5), that at first Adam spanned “behind and before,” meaning everywhere, and then God laid His hand on him and diminished him.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 38b) to illuminate his statement here (“(as stated in Sanhedrin 38b), meaning that he was certainly created circumcised, and through the corruption he became stretched in his foreskin; and since this occurred on the sixth day within the days of Creation,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And from this was forged the root for the birth of gentiles as uncircumcised, all being descendants of Adam HaRishon. column9: Psalms 90:4. English translation of source: “‘For a thousand years in Your sight are like yesterday when it has passed, and like a watch in the night.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok uses this verse as the scriptural basis for the aggadic analogy in which a millennium corresponds to a day. He then places the sixth millennium alongside the sixth day of creation and the sixth middah, yesod. That numerical and kabbalistic mapping is his developed interpretation rather than a literal calendar calculation supplied by the verse.

column9: Sanhedrin 97a. English translation of source: “‘Rav Ketina said: The world lasts six thousand years, and for one [thousand years] it is desolate, as it says, ‘And the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day’ [Isaiah 2:11]. Abaye said: For two [thousand years] it is desolate, as it says, ‘After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, and we shall live before Him’ [Hosea 6:2].’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok cites the seven-thousand-year pattern and relates it to the six days of creation followed by Shabbos. His further division of the millennia according to divine attributes supplies the conceptual bridge to Noach’s six-hundredth year. The passage should be read as theological symbolism within the rabbinic discussion, not as an independently verified prediction.
column11: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek 3-1:13 (§2): “And so was the historic order of the world: two thousand years of void (Tohu), followed by two thousand years of Torah (Sanhedrin 97a); but for one who stands in the daylight, daytime work comes first, followed by the night to rest from his labor; and likewise, once the Torah was given at Sinai, eternal illumination filled the cosmos, such that light takes precedence over darkness.” Connection to this note: In Dover Tzedek 3-1:13 (§2), Rav Tzadok develops the parallel foundation illuminating Exodus 12:2 and the teaching in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

column13: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Kedoshim 16:8: “This is why this first order is used with the commandment (Vayikra, 20:27), “a man or woman who has a familiar or is a wizard.”Even though it has already been written (Vayikra, 19:31), “do not turn to the familiars,” this additional verse comes so that one would not say, “I know the meaning of the mitzvot, for a familiar, ov, comes from the word for father, av, as in, ‘a father in wisdom,’” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Kedoshim 16:8 sheds direct light on Exodus 12:2 and Rav Tzadok's exposition in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.
